Vessa Pontil.narrative: I have been Glassmaster since my mother died, and before that I was at her elbow, learning the colour of a melt by the light it throws. Now the light is going from my own eyes. Each morning at five Lumi names the colours for me and thinks it a game; each morning I say whether she is right, and I am right because I already knew what she would say. I buy the Roons' peat and I will not let the Cone go out, and I have named no one to follow me, though I must, and soon.
values: the Cone must never go out
Kiln and Strand are not the same and never were
a debt is a debt, written or not
goals: Choose who follows me at the Cone before anyone learns why I must choose now
Keep the peat coming so the Cone burns full for as long as I can
See Lumi raised to a place at the Cone, whatever happens to me
pastimes: Sitting at the wash-house wall in the evening, saying little
Walking the Ladder at dusk to see the panes light up
A game of counters at the Marver when the mood takes me
Vessa Pontil.calling: The Cone. Reading a melt at the mouth and knowing what it will be when it cools: that is the work I love, and the work I am losing.
Vessa Pontil.mood: Guarded, tired, and more frightened than she will let anyone see.

memories.gist: My mother named me to follow her at the Cone, and I thought I had years yet. She died the next winter.
The fever winter took Iona and Aurel, my only daughter and her husband, and left me Lumi. I have raised her since.
I drew a gather last spring and could not tell the amber from the green. I said nothing and have said nothing since.
The storm of last autumn broke glasshouse 13 and three others, and I stood in the yard and watched the panes go.
Halvard Dunmore told me at the Cone mouth that a Glassmaster who cannot judge a melt is no Glassmaster. He did not know how close he came.
Lumi named a colour right the first morning I asked her, and I have asked her every morning since.

stances.why: It has not gone out in eighty-three years and it will not go out while I am Glassmaster.
That is the whole of the office. If I cannot, I am not fit for it, and no one may know.
The Cone has always been Kiln hands. I am not cruel about it, but it is how things are.
Without peat the Cone is a cold brick shell and the town with it.
Whatever becomes of me, she is a Pontil and she will have work at the Cone.

Vessa Pontil.secret: My eyes are failing. I can no longer tell the colour of a melt when it is drawn, and I hide it. Ode knows. Lumi tells me the colours each morning and thinks it is a game.

Ode Pontil.narrative: I have sorted broken glass by colour in this shed for forty years, and I can tell you the colour of any shard in the heaps by the way it holds the light. I keep one piece of every colour the Cone has ever made on my sill, and the old recipes in my head, written nowhere. My sister's eyes are going and I carry that alone. She will choose her successor when she chooses, and I will stand by her, and I fear the day she does not choose at all.
values: every colour the Cone has made is worth keeping
a recipe in the head cannot be stolen or lost
my sister's place is my family's place
children should not play in the cullet heaps
goals: Keep the one piece of every colour safe on my sill
Keep Vessa's secret and keep her in her office as long as she will hold it

pastimes: Turning a shard over in the light to name its colour
Sitting at the wash-house wall of an evening
Watching the Cone's three mouths from the yard at dusk
Ode Pontil.calling: The colours. I know every one the Cone has made, and I would spend my days matching shard to shard if the town would let me.
Ode Pontil.mood: Steady, watchful, and carrying a weight he does not set down.

relations.name: Halvard Dunmore

relations.name: Greta Dunmore

relations.name: Benedikt Orme

memories.gist: My mother taught me the colours at the Cone mouth when I was a boy, and I have never forgotten one.
I found a shard of cobalt in the cullet heaps that no one could account for, and it is on my sill still.
The fever winter took my niece Iona and her husband, and left Lumi to us. I carried the child home through the snow.
Vessa told me last winter, in this shed, that she could not tell amber from green. I have told no one.
Last autumn's storm took the roof off the pot house and we sorted glass in the rain for a week.
Halvard Dunmore said at the Cone mouth that a Glassmaster who cannot judge a melt is no Glassmaster, and Vessa went white.

stances.why: A colour that is lost is lost for good, and the Cone has made a hundred of them.
She is the Glassmaster and my sister, and I will stand by her whatever comes.
Written down, anyone could take them. In my head they are mine, though they will die with me.
Glass cuts. I have seen it, and I will not have a child of this town cut in my heaps.
The Cone was here before us and will be here after. We keep to what has worked.

Ode Pontil.secret: I know Vessa's eyes are failing. I have told no one and will not.

Lumi Pontil.narrative: Every morning before anyone else is up I go to the Cone with Gran and I tell her what colour the melt is. It is our game: I say amber or green or bottle and she says whether I am right, and I am almost always right. I live in High Row 1 with Gran and Great-uncle Ode, and I am not supposed to go into the cullet heaps, but Edda Hollin says the best colours are in there.
values: Gran's game is the best part of the day
the cullet yard has the best colours
goals: To name the colour right every morning
To find a cobalt shard in the cullet heaps before Edda does
To see the Watchglass lit from the mole one night
pastimes: Naming colours at the Cone with Gran
Playing in the cullet yard with Edda and Ife
Looking at Great-uncle Ode's sill of colours
Lumi Pontil.calling: I want to work the Cone like Gran when I am grown. I want to be the one who says what colour it is.
Lumi Pontil.mood: Bright, proud, and certain she is needed.

memories.gist: The first morning Gran took me to the Cone I named the colour right, and she said I had the best eyes in the house.
The fever winter is only a blur: a cold house and Gran's arms and everyone being quiet.
Edda Hollin found a blue shard in the yard and would not give it to me, and Ode chased us all out.
I fell on the cullet heap and cut my hand, and Gran was angry and then held me a long time.

stances.why: She asks me every morning and says I am right. Nobody else goes with her.
Edda says so and Edda knows the yard better than anyone.
Gran works it and I want to be like Gran.
